gtrig-siblings-special-sums#1.en:
Answer this ENTIRE question WITHOUT using a calculator.
It is given that  5 sin θ + 3 = 0  and  cos θ > 0.

Draw a sketch and determine the length of the third side of your triangle.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#2.en: Step ① never changes: get the ratio on its own. Then draw your cross and tick it twice — once for the quadrants where sin is negative, once for the quadrants where cos is positive. The quadrant that collects two ticks is the one you sketch in, and (pyth) finds the side that is missing.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#3.en: ① Isolate the function:  5 sin θ = −3  ⟹  sin θ = −3/5

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#4.en: ② Determine the quadrant. Tick the cross twice: sin θ is negative in III and IV; cos θ is positive in I and IV. The quadrant with two ticks wins — IV.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#5.en: ③ Sketch it in the fourth quadrant, with  y = −3  and  r = 5.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#7.en: In the fourth quadrant x is positive  ∴  x = 4

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#8.en: WATCH OUT: r never takes a minus — it is the radius, and a radius is a length. Only x and y carry the quadrant's signs.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#9.en: Special sums run on five numbered steps, and step ② is where the whole teaching sits. Step ① is quick: 5 sin θ = −3, so sin θ = −3 over 5. Now draw the little cross and tick it twice, in two colours if that helps you see it. Sine is negative in III and IV. Cosine is positive in I and IV. The quadrant that collected two ticks wins, and that is IV. All Strippers Take Cash says the same thing round the bow tie, but the double tick is the reason the step exists — sin θ = −3 over 5 on its own fits two quadrants, and those two would hand you opposite answers. After that the sketch does the work: y = −3, r = 5, and (pyth) gives 4 for the side that is left. The quadrant tells you to write it as +4, because in IV the x is positive.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#10.en: Hence, without using a calculator, determine the value of  tan θ · cos θ

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#11.en: Everything you need is on the sketch now. tan is y over x and cos is x over r — read the two straight off, signs and all, and multiply.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#12.en: ⑤ Substitute. Read the ratios off the sketch:  tan θ = y/x = −3/4

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#15.en: REMEMBER: the answer came out as exactly sin θ, the thing you were given — and that is not luck. tan is sin over cos, so tan θ · cos θ is always sin θ. Treat it as a free check on your arithmetic.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#16.en: Once the triangle is drawn, every ratio is two of its three numbers divided, and the calculator stays in your bag. tan θ is y over x, so −3 over 4. cos θ is x over r, so 4 over 5. Multiply them and the 4s cancel, leaving −3 over 5. Look at what that is: −3 over 5 is sin θ, the very thing you were given at the start. That is not luck. tan is sin over cos, so tan θ times cos θ is always sin θ, whatever the numbers are. Answers that fold back onto something you already know are a free check — if your product had come out as anything other than −3 over 5, you would know a sign had gone astray somewhere.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#17.en:
Answer this ENTIRE question WITHOUT using a calculator.
It is given that  tan θ = −5/12  and  θ ∈ (90° ; 270°).

Draw a sketch and determine the length of the hypotenuse of your triangle.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#18.en: tan θ = y over x, so the minus could sit on either the top or the bottom. Let the quadrant decide which. Tick the cross twice — once for where tan is negative, once for the interval you were given.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#19.en: ① The function is already on its own:  tan θ = −5/12

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#20.en: ② Determine the quadrant. Tick the cross twice: tan θ is negative in II and IV; θ ∈ (90° ; 270°) allows II and III. The double tick lands on II.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#21.en: ③ Sketch it in the second quadrant. tan θ = y/x, and in II the x is negative while the y is positive  ∴  x = −12  and  y = 5.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#23.en: r = 13  — always positive, because it is the radius

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#24.en: WATCH OUT: tan θ = −5/12 does NOT automatically mean y = −5 and x = 12. The quadrant decides which of the two carries the minus — in II it is the x. Put it on the wrong one and every answer after it flips sign.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#25.en: This one is given as a tan, and a tan hides an extra decision: tan θ is y over x, so the minus could belong to either the top or the bottom. That is exactly what the quadrant step settles. Tan is negative in II and IV. The interval from 90° to 270° allows II and III. Two ticks land on II, and in the second quadrant x is negative while y is positive — so y = 5 and x = −12, not the other way round. Then Pythagoras finds the hypotenuse: r² = (−12)² + 5², which is 169, so r = 13. Notice that r never takes a minus, because r is the radius and a radius is a length. Write the negative coordinate inside the square, the way she does, and you will not lose track of which one it was.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#26.en: Hence, without using a calculator, determine the value of  sin θ + cos θ

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#27.en: Both ratios have the same r underneath, so once you have written them down the adding is easy. Read the signs off the sketch, not off the original equation.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#28.en: ⑤ Substitute. Read both ratios off the sketch:  sin θ = y/r = 5/13

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#31.en: With the triangle drawn there is nothing left to decide — sin θ is y over r and cos θ is x over r, so the answers are 5 over 13 and −12 over 13. Adding them gives −7 over 13. Two habits keep this part clean. The first is reading each ratio off the picture rather than off the original equation, because the picture already has the signs built into it. The second is noticing that both ratios share the same r, so they share the same denominator all the way through — if your two fractions have different bottoms, something has gone wrong. And a quick sense check: in the second quadrant sine is positive and cosine is negative, and here the cosine is the bigger of the two in size, so a small NEGATIVE answer is exactly what you should expect.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#32.en:
Answer this ENTIRE question WITHOUT using a calculator.
P(−2 ; −3) is a point on the terminal arm of θ.

Draw a sketch and determine the length of OP, leaving your answer in surd form.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#33.en: A point does step ② for you — the two signs already say which quadrant you are in. From there it is (pyth) on the little triangle you drop down to the x-axis.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#34.en: The point tells you the quadrant straight away: both coordinates are negative, so P lies in the third quadrant, with  x = −2  and  y = −3.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#36.en: OP = √13  — always positive, because it is the radius

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#37.en: When the question hands you a point instead of a ratio, step ② is already done for you — there is no sign reasoning to do at all, because the coordinates say where the point is. Both of P's coordinates are negative, so P is in the third quadrant, bottom left. From there it is plain Pythagoras on the little triangle you drop down to the x-axis: OP² = (−2)² + (−3)², which is 4 + 9 = 13, so OP is √13. Leave it as a surd; turning it into a decimal here would spoil every ratio that comes next. And OP is always positive, because it is the radius — the minus signs live on x and y only, never on the distance from the origin.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#38.en: Hence, without using a calculator, determine the values of  sin θ,  cos θ  and  tan θ. Rationalise any surd in a denominator.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#39.en: Three ratios, three pairs of numbers from the same sketch. Leave the surd in place while you write them down, then rationalise anything with a √ underneath the line.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#43.en: REMEMBER: two negatives divided give a positive, so tan θ comes out POSITIVE in the third quadrant — which is exactly what All Strippers Take Cash promises (T is the tan quadrant). If yours came out negative, check the signs on your sketch.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#44.en: Three ratios, three pairs of numbers off the same sketch. sin θ is y over r, which is −3 over √13. cos θ is x over r, which is −2 over √13. tan θ is y over x, and two negatives divided give a positive, so it is 3 over 2. Then comes her one rule about surds: a special-sums answer gets rationalised, even though a special-angle value like 1 over √3 is left alone. Multiply top and bottom by √13 and −3 over √13 becomes −3√13 over 13. Last, use the wheel as a check. This is the third quadrant, T on All Strippers Take Cash, so tan should come out positive and the other two negative — and they do.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#45.en:
Answer this ENTIRE question WITHOUT using a calculator.
It is given that  25 cos θ = −24  and  θ ∈ (180° ; 360°).

Draw a sketch and determine the length of the third side of your triangle.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#46.en: Divide by 25 first, then tick the cross twice — once for where cos is negative, once for the interval. Keep the given negative coordinate inside the square when you do (pyth).

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#48.en: ② Determine the quadrant. Tick the cross twice: cos θ is negative in II and III; θ ∈ (180° ; 360°) allows III and IV. The double tick lands on III.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#49.en: ③ Sketch it in the third quadrant, with  x = −24  and  r = 25.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#51.en: In the third quadrant y is negative  ∴  y = −7

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#52.en: WATCH OUT: the given negative coordinate stays INSIDE the square — write 25² − (−24)², not 625 − 576 straight off. It costs one extra line and it keeps you honest about which number was negative.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#53.en: Same five steps, bigger numbers. Step ①: divide by 25 to get cos θ on its own, giving −24 over 25. Step ②: tick the cross twice. Cosine is negative in II and III. The interval from 180° to 360° allows III and IV. The double tick lands on III. Step ③: sketch it bottom left, with x = −24 and r = 25. Step ④: Pythagoras, and write the negative coordinate inside the square the way she does — y² = 25² − (−24)² gives 49, so y is ±7, and the third quadrant picks the negative one. The ± line followed by a ∴ line is not decoration: it is where you show the marker that the quadrant, not the calculator, chose the sign.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#54.en: Hence, without using a calculator, determine the value of  24 tan θ − 25 sin θ

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#55.en: Read tan and sin straight off the sketch, and look at the numbers sitting in front of them — 24 and 25 are there for a reason.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#56.en: ⑤ Substitute. Read the ratios off the sketch:  tan θ = y/x = (−7)/(−24) = 7/24

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#59.en: Everything now comes off the picture. tan θ is y over x, and −7 over −24 is a positive 7 over 24, exactly as the third quadrant promised. sin θ is y over r, which is −7 over 25. Then substitute carefully: 24 times 7 over 24 is 7, and 25 times −7 over 25 is −7, so subtracting the second from the first gives 7 + 7 = 14. The numbers in front, 24 and 25, were chosen to cancel the denominators, and that is worth noticing — when the coefficient matches the bottom of the ratio, the arithmetic is about to be tidy, so a messy answer usually means a sign slipped somewhere.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#60.en: Hence, without using a calculator, determine the value of  25 cos(180° + θ) + 25 sin(180° − θ)

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#61.en: Reduce both angles before you read anything off the sketch. And be careful with the second one: leaving sin θ unchanged does not make it positive.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#62.en: 180° + θ lands in T, where only tan is positive, so cosine turns negative:  cos(180° + θ) = −cos θ = 24/25

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#63.en: 180° − θ lands in S, where sine is positive, so sine keeps its own value:  sin(180° − θ) = sin θ = −7/25

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#65.en: WATCH OUT: “sin(180° − θ) = sin θ” does not mean the answer is positive. The reduction leaves sin θ exactly as it was — and on this sketch sin θ was already negative.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#66.en: Two reductions, and then the same picture as before. 180° + θ lands in T, where only tan survives, so cosine picks up a minus and cos(180° + θ) is −cos θ, which is a positive 24 over 25. 180° − θ lands in S, where sine survives, so sin(180° − θ) is simply sin θ — and sin θ is already −7 over 25 on this sketch. That is the sentence worth reading twice: the reduction did not make it positive, it left it exactly as it was, and it was negative to begin with. Multiply each by 25, add them, and you get 24 − 7 = 17. Reduce first, then read the sketch, and never try to do both on one line.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#67.en:
Answer this ENTIRE question WITHOUT using a calculator.
M(4 ; −1) is a point on the terminal arm of θ, where θ is a reflex angle measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis.

Draw a sketch and determine the length of OM, leaving your answer in surd form.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#68.en: Reflex just means θ has turned past 180°. Plot M first, see which quadrant it lands in, then use (pyth) on the triangle you drop down to the x-axis.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#69.en: M(4 ; −1) has a positive x and a negative y, so it sits in the fourth quadrant — which is what makes θ reflex: turning anticlockwise you pass 90°, 180° and 270° before you reach OM.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#71.en: OM = √17  — always positive, because it is the radius

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#72.en: A reflex angle just means θ has turned more than halfway round. M sits in the fourth quadrant, so turning anticlockwise from the positive x-axis you sweep past 90°, past 180°, past 270° and only then reach OM — which puts θ somewhere between 270° and 360°. That is all the word reflex is telling you here, and it agrees with the quadrant the coordinates already gave you. The rest is Pythagoras on the little triangle dropped down to the x-axis: OM² = 4² + (−1)², which is 17, so OM is √17. Leave it as a surd, and keep it positive — the distance from the origin has no sign.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#73.en: Hence, without using a calculator, determine the value of  cos(180° − θ)

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#74.en: One reduction, then one read-off. And remember her rule about surds: a special-sums answer gets rationalised.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#75.en: 180° − θ lands in S, where only sine is positive, so cosine takes the minus:  cos(180° − θ) = −cos θ

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#76.en: Read cos θ off the sketch:  cos θ = x/r = 4/√17

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#78.en: REMEMBER: special-ANGLE values are left as 1/√3 and 1/√2, but a special-SUMS answer gets rationalised — multiply top and bottom by √17 so nothing awkward is left under the line.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#79.en: Two moves. First the reduction: 180° − θ lands in S, where only sine is positive, and cosine is not sine, so it takes the minus and cos(180° − θ) = −cos θ. Second, read cos θ off the sketch: it is x over r, which is 4 over √17. Put them together and you have −4 over √17. Then rationalise, because that is what she does with a special-sums answer even though she leaves a special-angle value like 1 over √3 alone. Multiply top and bottom by √17 and you get −4√17 over 17. It looks bigger, but it is the same number with nothing awkward left underneath the line.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#80.en: Hence, without using a calculator, determine the value of  1 − sin²(180° + θ)

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#81.en: Look at the shape of the expression before you reduce anything. 1 minus a sine squared is a masked identity waiting to happen.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#82.en: Start with the masked identity, read backwards:  1 − sin²A = cos²A,  so  1 − sin²(180° + θ) = cos²(180° + θ)

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#83.en: Now reduce inside block brackets before squaring:  cos(180° + θ) = −cos θ,  so  cos²(180° + θ) = [−cos θ]² = cos²θ

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#85.en: WATCH OUT: squaring kills the minus. [−cos θ]² is +cos²θ, never −cos²θ. That one sign is the whole difference between 16/17 and its negative.

gtrig-siblings-special-sums#86.en: Do not reduce first here — look at the shape of the expression instead. 1 minus a sine squared is one of her masked identities read backwards, so 1 − sin²(180° + θ) becomes cos²(180° + θ) before any reduction happens at all. That single move saves you most of the work. Now reduce inside block brackets: 180° + θ is in T, so cosine turns negative and you have that bracket squared. Squaring kills the minus, so it is plain cos²θ. Finally read cos θ off the sketch, 4 over √17, and square it: 16 over 17. Notice the answer needed no rationalising, because squaring the √17 turned it into an ordinary 17 all by itself.
